title: Password Checker and Generator following NIST SP 800-63B
description:
A small Python tool that generates passwords and passphrases with the secrets module and checks existing passwords the way NIST SP 800-63B (revision 4) asks password verifiers to.

  • Length over composition: at least 15 characters (8 if the password is one factor of MFA), spaces and Unicode allowed, no character-class rules.
  • Breach check: lookup in Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords corpus through the k-anonymity range API. Only the first 5 characters of the SHA-1 hash are sent.
  • Strength estimate: zxcvbn detects dictionary words, keyboard walks, dates, repeats and l33t substitutions and explains why a password is weak.

No machine-learning model is needed: the checks are deterministic and explainable.
aiTools: Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords API
implementationSteps: Normalize the password to Unicode NFC and count its length in code points
Require at least 15 characters (8 when used with MFA) and accept up to 128, without composition rules
Hash with SHA-1, send only the first 5 hex characters to api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/ with padding enabled, and compare the suffixes locally
Run zxcvbn with account-specific words (name, email) and reject scores below 3 of 4
Return a verdict with the concrete problems and zxcvbn's suggestions
Generate passphrases from the 7,776-word EFF list and random passwords with secrets.choice, and report their entropy
Test offline: mock the range API with httpx.MockTransport and check every rule with fixed passwords
performance:
Expectations, not measurements:

  • One check takes one HTTPS request to the range API plus milliseconds of local work; zxcvbn analyzes at most the first 100 characters to stay fast.
  • A 6-word passphrase from the EFF list has about 77.5 bits of entropy; a 20-character password from the 72-character default alphabet about 123 bits.
  • zxcvbn's score is an estimate based on mostly English dictionaries, not a guarantee.
userExperience: The user enters a password at a hidden prompt and gets a clear verdict: accepted or not, length, zxcvbn strength (0 to 4), how often it was found in breaches, and specific suggestions such as "Add another word or two". The generator prints a passphrase and its entropy. The same functions can sit behind a sign-up form for a live strength meter.
